stories.headline: Blind Dunedin Woman and Her Friend Finish Walking All 2000-Plus Streets in Greater Dunedin
stories.summary: Julie Woods, who is blind, and her friend Jo Stodart spent six and a half years walking every street in Greater Dunedin, one Saturday morning at a time, joined by a hot pink rope. They finished in October and say they hope to inspire others to get out walking.
stories.narrative:
Two friends of 33 years in Dunedin have just finished a project that took them six and a half years: walking every street in Greater Dunedin.

Julie Woods is 60 and blind. Jo Stodart is 62, sighted, and works as an infection prevention nurse manager. Starting in March 2019, they set out each Saturday morning, early in the day, for walks of about an hour. First came the more than a thousand streets of the inner city, spread over 44 hilly suburbs. Then they moved on to another thousand or so across 58 more suburbs, in a region of more than three thousand square kilometres.

Their system is simple. Jo drives them to a chosen suburb, plans where to park so they never repeat a street, and walks in front. A short hot pink rope links the two of them, and Jo only speaks up when the ground turns dangerous. Julie keeps a spreadsheet of the streets still to do. When strangers offered unsolicited advice on how they should walk, they settled on a motto: our goal, our rules.

They finished on the eleventh of October. Rain, they say, only got in the way about once every three months. Both describe finding beauty in the ordinary: the sound of the sea, paddocks full of sheep, and friendly train crews in Green Island and Port Chalmers.

The pair say the friendship is what kept it going, especially on mornings when getting out of bed was hard. Jo hopes they have encouraged others, and says that if they get even one person off the couch and out walking, that is a good thing. They don't yet know what their next project will be.

stories.headline: Wellington's Ōtari-Wilton's Bush, the World's First Native Plant Museum, Celebrates 100 Years
stories.summary: Ōtari-Wilton's Bush marked a century since it opened as New Zealand's native plant garden. It now holds about half of the country's flora and relies on volunteers who put in more hours than paid staff.
stories.narrative:
Wellington's Ōtari-Wilton's Bush has turned 100. It opened on the twelfth of October 1926 as an open-air native plant museum, described as the first of its kind in the world.

It began with one settler. Job Wilton bought land in the Kaiwharawhara Valley by 1860 and fenced off seventeen acres of untouched forest to protect it. The area was gazetted as a forest reserve in 1906. Botanist Leonard Cockayne then lobbied for a place to grow and study native plants, and city park supervisor John Gretton Mackenzie, nicknamed Pōhutukawa Mac, helped make it happen.

Today the site covers more than a hundred hectares, mostly protected podocarp and broadleaf forest, with about five hectares of planted collections. It holds around 1,100 kinds of plants, roughly half of New Zealand's flora, and each one has records of where it came from, which helps research and conservation.

The garden's plant conservation lab works with the Department of Conservation to grow threatened orchids, including one of the country's rarest, for return to the wild. Volunteers are a big part of the story too. Their recent hours add up to more than seven full-time staff, which is more than the number of paid staff.

stories.headline: 126 Acres of Cape Cod Salt Marsh Returned to Native American Ownership Near First Encounter Beach
stories.summary: The Nature Conservancy has given about 126 acres in Eastham, Massachusetts to the Indigenous-led Native Land Conservancy. The land protects salt marsh habitat and will be used for traditional foraging, fishing and ceremony.
stories.narrative:
On the thirtieth of October, The Nature Conservancy handed about 126 acres of salt marsh and coastal habitat in Eastham, on Cape Cod, to the Native Land Conservancy, an Indigenous-led nonprofit based in Mashpee.

The land sits beside a 20-acre parcel that the group bought in June for three million dollars, with help from a local conservation foundation and neighbours. Together they form a larger protected area overlooking First Encounter Beach, where in December 1620 colonists and Nauset warriors clashed soon after the Pilgrims arrived.

Conservation rules will limit development on parts of the land, while still allowing traditional uses such as aquaculture. Plans include removing invasive plants and restoring native species for cultural and ceremonial use. The marsh also shelters wildlife such as diamondback terrapins, which nest on the coastal bluffs.

Founder Ramona Peters, a Mashpee Wampanoag member, called the return an act of resilience after four centuries of dispossession. The organisation, founded in 2012, now holds more than twenty properties across Massachusetts, and its board represents seven tribes.

stories.headline: Jonathan the 194-Year-Old Tortoise Reveals Genetic Clues to a Long, Healthy Life
stories.summary: Scientists studied Jonathan, an Aldabra giant tortoise thought to be 194 and the oldest known living land animal. They found 287 genetic variants tied to DNA repair and cancer suppression, and his gene regulation looks much like that of far younger tortoises.
stories.narrative:
Jonathan, a giant tortoise on the island of St Helena, is believed to have hatched in 1832, which makes him the oldest known living land animal. Researchers have now studied his genes to find out how he has lasted so long.

The study, published in Science Advances, is the first look at the epigenome of a giant tortoise, meaning the chemical markers that switch genes on and off. The team compared Jonathan with younger tortoises of the same species.

They found 287 distinctive genetic variants linked to protection against ageing. These touch on DNA repair, inflammation, insulin regulation and cancer suppression. Systems for DNA repair and metabolism stayed remarkably stable in him, closely resembling those of much younger relatives.

The researchers hope this could eventually inform ways to slow age-related decline in people, though they stress that is a long way off and needs more research.

stories.headline: Releasing Wolbachia Mosquitoes Cuts Dengue by 68% in Brazilian Randomised Trial
stories.summary: A randomised trial in Belo Horizonte found that releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria cut dengue cases by 68.5% and chikungunya by 73.3% among schoolchildren. The results came during Brazil's largest recorded dengue outbreak.
stories.narrative:
A large trial in Brazil has produced some of the strongest evidence yet that a clever biological trick can protect people from mosquito-borne disease.

Researchers in the city of Belo Horizonte divided the area around schools into 58 clusters. In half of them, they released mosquitoes carrying a harmless bacterium called Wolbachia, which stops the insects from passing on viruses. The other half relied on standard control measures such as spraying and removing breeding sites. More than five thousand schoolchildren aged six to eleven were followed.

The releases ran from early 2021 to mid 2022, a period that overlapped with the biggest dengue outbreak Brazil has ever recorded. Even so, dengue cases fell by about 68 percent in the areas with Wolbachia mosquitoes, and chikungunya cases dropped by around 73 percent. There were too few Zika cases to measure.

The findings were presented at a tropical medicine meeting in Maryland by a team from Johns Hopkins, the Federal University of Minas Gerais, the World Mosquito Program and other institutions. A citywide trial in Singapore has reported a similar drop.

What makes this good news is that the approach is self-sustaining: once the bacteria establish in local mosquitoes, protection keeps going without constant spraying. For cities where dengue sends hundreds of thousands of people to hospital each year, that is a real prospect of lasting relief.

stories.headline: Yap Island School Accepts Coconuts Instead of Tuition Fees
stories.summary: Faith Christian Academy on Yap in Micronesia lets families pay school fees in coconuts, which feed a new virgin coconut oil business. The scheme eases pressure on families where few have cash incomes, and organisers plan to extend it to other schools and islands.
stories.narrative:
On the island of Yap in the Federated States of Micronesia, a school has found a way to make education affordable without requiring cash that most families simply do not have.

Only about a third of islanders have paid work, mostly with the government, and the old coconut oil export trade faded away decades ago. Some students had been fishing at night to help cover fees, and some parents were working double shifts.

Faith Christian Academy now accepts coconuts in place of tuition. The nuts go to a company called Island VCO, which presses high-grade virgin coconut oil. Because Yap bans pesticides, the coconuts are naturally organic, and the company is working toward certification and preparing its first shipments.

Students say gathering coconuts is rewarding and social, and one said her father no longer has to work so much to pay for her schooling. Profits beyond costs go to a nonprofit working in the Pacific.

Organisers plan to offer the arrangement to other private schools on Yap and then to other islands in Micronesia and the Marshall Islands, turning a plentiful local resource into schooling for kids.

stories.headline: Northland's First Wind Farm, Kaiwaikawe, Officially Opens
stories.summary: Mercury has opened the $287 million Kaiwaikawe wind farm, with 12 turbines expected to power about 31,000 homes. It was built on time and on budget with no serious accidents, and includes funding for protecting the endangered bittern.
stories.narrative:
Northland now has its first wind farm. Mercury officially opened the Kaiwaikawe project on the 23rd of November, with twelve turbines standing over land owned by Pāmu and within the rohe of Te Roroa.

Each turbine reaches 206 metres to the blade tip and can generate up to six megawatts. Together they produce 77 megawatts, expected to be around 220 gigawatt hours a year, enough for roughly 31,000 homes. The first turbines began feeding power into the grid in July, with final commissioning to run into early 2027.

The project cost 287 million dollars and was reported as on time and on budget. At peak, about 180 people worked on site each day, clocking more than a quarter of a million hours without a serious accident.

There is also a conservation component: a 640,000 dollar fund for DOC and iwi programmes protecting the endangered matuku-hūrepo, the bittern, plus 360,000 dollars for GPS tracking, and 30,000 dollars a year for a local community fund.

It is a concrete addition of clean, local electricity for the north, delivered with iwi involvement.

stories.headline: Eleven Chevron Skinks Return to Great Barrier Island After 30 Years in Auckland Zoo's Care
stories.summary: Eleven niho taniwha, New Zealand's longest lizard, have been released into Glenfern Sanctuary on Aotea/Great Barrier Island. They join ten released in July, and the species survives on only two islands.
stories.narrative:
Eleven chevron skinks, known in te reo Māori as niho taniwha, have gone home to Aotea, also called Great Barrier Island, after three decades of Auckland Zoo looking after their line.

The story began between 1997 and 1999, when three injured skinks were taken from the island to the zoo for rehabilitation. From those animals the zoo built up a group of 21, made up of the two original adults and 19 zoo-bred skinks. At up to thirty centimetres from nose to tail, the niho taniwha is New Zealand's longest lizard, and it is classed as nationally vulnerable. It now lives only on Aotea and on Te Hauturu-o-Toi, Little Barrier Island.

The skinks were released into Glenfern Sanctuary, where predators are controlled. They join ten others released there in July, bringing the total to twenty-one. Researchers have fitted small transmitters to their tails so they can follow where the secretive lizards go, and a Unitec master's student is part of that work. The zoo says the releases should teach scientists a great deal about how this elusive species behaves.

The project is a partnership between Ngāti Rehua Ngātiwai ki Aotea Trust, the Department of Conservation, Auckland Zoo, Glenfern Sanctuary and Auckland Council. Kaumātua Rodney Ngāwaka described the niho taniwha as one of the iwi's most precious taonga, unique to their rohe.

It is good news because a species that survives in just two places now has more animals living back in the wild on the island where the zoo's founders were found, after thirty years of patient breeding.

stories.headline: 'Retired' Pair of Critically Endangered Kākāriki Karaka Surprise Keepers With Two Clutches of Eggs
stories.summary: Orange-fronted parakeets Sophia and Prince Polo at Orana Wildlife Park had been retired from breeding because of their age. They have now raised chicks and laid a second clutch, a boost for a species with only about 450 birds left.
stories.narrative:
A pair of critically endangered parakeets that were supposed to be enjoying retirement have instead delivered a double surprise for conservationists.

Sophia and Prince Polo are kākāriki karaka, or orange-fronted parakeets, living at Orana Wildlife Park in Christchurch. Because of their age, they had been officially retired from breeding and moved to a display area. Sophia had first been paired with a male called Poldark, and after he died she was matched with Prince Polo.

Then Sophia laid a clutch of eggs. About four weeks later, while those chicks were still a month old, she laid a second clutch in the same nest box. Prince Polo is now feeding chicks that are four months old. The park's native fauna manager said the magic simply happened.

The birds matter well beyond their own nest. The kākāriki karaka has been declared extinct twice, and only about 450 remain, mostly on offshore islands or at the Brook Waimārama Sanctuary near Nelson, with a small remnant in Canterbury. Sophia and Prince Polo were taken as eggs from wild nests in the Poulter Valley around eight years ago, so they carry valuable genetics.

The Department of Conservation's recovery programme lead called the pair breeding a huge win. For a species this rare, every healthy chick with good genes is a real step forward.

stories.headline: Nearly 50,000 Acres in Alaska Secured as Permanent Refuge for Pacific Walrus
stories.summary: The Conservation Fund has signed a deal with an Alaska Native corporation to protect barrier islands near Point Lay, where more than 200,000 walruses haul out each fall. The agreement restricts development and disturbance on the land.
stories.narrative:
A huge stretch of Alaska's Arctic coast has been protected for the walruses that rely on it.

Each fall, more than 200,000 Pacific walruses crowd onto barrier islands near the village of Point Lay, in northwest Alaska. It is the largest walrus haulout in North America. The gathering began in 2007, when shrinking sea ice left a few thousand females and calves looking for somewhere to rest, and now nearly all Pacific walrus females and their young use the site.

The Conservation Fund has agreed a deal with the Cully Corporation, the Alaska Native village corporation that owns the land, to secure close to 50,000 acres as a permanent refuge. The agreement limits resource development and other human activity, and Cully receives a payment aimed at community well-being, though the amount has not been disclosed. The work took roughly ten years to build.

The main danger to the animals is stampedes. Walruses weighing up to two tons can be spooked by planes, ships, tourists or polar bears, and young animals are sometimes crushed. Point Lay also sits on the edge of the National Petroleum Reserve, an area eyed for oil and gas.

A Conservation Fund spokesperson said big animals need even bigger landscapes, and another described the project as adaptation in real time. For a species pushed ashore by a changing climate, a guaranteed safe place to rest is a concrete, lasting win.

stories.headline: World's First Museum Built Inside a Children's Hospital Opens in New Orleans, Fulfilling a Dying Boy's Wish
stories.summary: Walker's Imaginarium, a 15,000-square-foot museum inside Manning Family Children's hospital, was inspired by nine-year-old Walker Beery, who wanted play during chemotherapy. It was funded entirely by donations.
stories.narrative:
A hospital in New Orleans now has a children's museum inside it, and it exists because of a boy who wanted to play during chemotherapy.

Walker Beery was diagnosed with a pediatric brain cancer in August 2019 and spent about two years in treatment at what is now Manning Family Children's. He died at the age of nine, but before then he and his family started a foundation called Kids Join The Fight to raise money for a place where patients could simply be kids.

The result is Walker's Imaginarium, a 15,000-square-foot museum that is described as the first of its kind inside a hospital. Its Louisiana-themed exhibits include a bayou with airboat rides, a Mardi Gras parade, a crawfish boil, a mini football field and a stage for dancing to cajun music. A terrace holds a nine-hole mini-golf course with an oversized alligator.

It is built for children with medical needs, with wheelchair-friendly play areas and sensory-aware design. A light-up butterfly responds to an accessible swing, and a classroom helps patients who miss school. The whole project was paid for by donations, and it has joined the Association of Children's Museums.

The hospital's chief executive said that even on the hardest days of a child's life there should be room for childhood. Walker's family says his spirit lives on in the joy of the place.

stories.headline: New Light Therapy Kills Gum Disease Bacteria While Sparing Beneficial Ones in Mice
stories.summary: Nagoya University researchers paired hen-egg antibodies with a light-activated dye to target the main gum disease pathogen. In mice, it cut bone loss and left healthy oral bacteria intact, though human trials are still to come.
stories.narrative:
Researchers in Japan have developed a gum disease treatment that picks out the villain and leaves the rest of the mouth's bacteria alone.

Periodontitis is driven largely by a bacterium called Porphyromonas gingivalis. Antibiotics and standard light therapies tend to hit the whole oral community, good microbes included. The team at Nagoya University instead used antibodies from egg yolks of hens immunised against the bacterium, attached to a light-sensitive dye. When near-infrared light is shone on the area, the dye damages the membranes of only the targeted bacteria.

In lab tests the combination stuck specifically to the problem bacterium, and did not affect other bacteria or healthy gum cells. In mice with periodontitis, it significantly reduced bone loss around the teeth and lowered levels of the pathogen in saliva while protecting helpful Streptococcus species. Older approaches disrupted the wider microbial community.

The work was published in the Journal of Translational Medicine. It is still experimental: it has only been tested in cell cultures and mice, and gum disease involves several bacteria, so more targets may be needed. The team plans to use AI to find them.

It is encouraging because it points to a more precise way to treat a very common condition.

stories.headline: Native Oysters Born in Scotland's Dornoch Firth for the First Time in Over a Century
stories.summary: Scientists monitoring a restoration reef in the Dornoch Firth found baby oysters, the first born there since the species was fished out in the 1800s. Experts at two national museums verified the find, which shows the 140,000-oyster project has created a self-sustaining population.
stories.narrative:
Native oysters have been born in Scotland's Dornoch Firth for the first time in more than a hundred years, and the discovery shows a long restoration effort is working.

The firth's oysters were most likely fished to extinction in the late nineteenth century. In 2017, scientists from Heriot-Watt University, working with the Glenmorangie distillery and the Marine Conservation Society, placed the first three hundred oysters on the seabed. Over twelve years, volunteers and researchers have bred, cleaned and released more than a hundred and forty thousand juvenile oysters.

The breakthrough came during routine monitoring. Research associate Gurjameer Ramday found tiny baby oysters, known as spat, on shells that the team had laid down to attract larvae. Specialists at National Museums Scotland and Museum Wales checked the images and confirmed what they were. On a later visit, some of the youngsters had grown to about the size of a fifty pence coin, which suggests they are thriving.

About three thousand oysters are now reaching maturity across two established beds. Project leader Professor Bill Sanderson called it a moment twelve years and a hundred and forty thousand oysters in the making. Ramday said that finding baby oysters is proof that targeted restoration can work, and noted that warm sea conditions in 2025 and 2026 may have helped.

This matters beyond the shellfish themselves. Oyster reefs filter water, store carbon and give shelter to many other species. The team hopes to reach around four million oysters by 2031, though that will need more funding, and the lessons will feed into oyster projects across the UK.

stories.headline: Hormone-Driven High Blood Pressure Eased for Up to Two Years After Drug Treatment Stopped
stories.summary: In a small study, people with blood pressure caused by excess aldosterone kept lower hormone levels and pressure for up to two years after stopping the FDA-approved drug baxdrostat. Some had normal blood pressure without any medication.
stories.narrative:
A drug already approved in the United States may be able to do more than manage one kind of high blood pressure. It may switch off its cause.

About five to ten percent of high blood pressure cases are driven by too much aldosterone, a hormone that makes the kidneys hold on to salt. Until now, the only way to cure this was surgery to remove an adrenal gland. Otherwise, patients took pills for life.

A team led by Professor Morris Brown at Queen Mary University of London gave the drug baxdrostat to fourteen people at eight American centres for six to twelve months, then followed them after treatment ended. The idea came from a mouse study in 2005, which suggested that blocking the hormone's production for long enough might cause the overactive cells to disappear.

The results were striking. A key marker of aldosterone stayed about ninety-nine percent lower than before treatment, and average blood pressure was around twenty-five points lower. The benefits lasted up to two years after people stopped the drug, and just under a quarter had completely normal blood pressure with no medication at all.

The study is small, and Brown is clear that this will not cure most people with hypertension, only those with this hormonal cause. A larger trial is now under way to see whether the effect holds. Still, it points to a future where some patients could stop taking pills, and avoid surgery.

stories.headline: Lake Baikal, the World's Largest Freshwater Lake, Is Recovering After Decades of Drying
stories.summary: Tree-ring research shows that river flow into Lake Baikal has been about 145% above its long-term average since 2017, with lake levels and vegetation rising. The researchers credit natural shifts in weather patterns.
stories.narrative:
Lake Baikal in Siberia holds roughly a fifth of the world's surface fresh water, and new research suggests it has been quietly recovering from a long decline.

Through the twentieth century, parts of East Asia grew steadily drier, and flow in the Selenga River, the lake's main source, fell by as much as ninety percent in the worst periods. Roughly half of all extreme drought years in the record came after 1900, which raised worries for wildlife and for the people who rely on the lake for drinking water, farming and power.

Researchers at Yunnan University, led by doctoral researcher Shijie Wang, studied rings in pine trees around the lake. Wide rings mean wet years and narrow rings mean dry ones, so 343 years of rings let them rebuild the river's flow across centuries.

The record shows a turnaround starting in 2017. Streamflow has since run about a hundred and forty-five percent above the long-term average, lake levels are rising, and more vegetation is growing around it.

The team links the change to shifting weather patterns that bring more moisture from northern seas, and to a slowdown in Arctic warming in some regions. They stress that this reflects natural variability, not a reversal of global warming, so it may not last. But it is welcome relief for one of the planet's most important and biodiverse lakes, and a reason to prepare, with better water storage and restored wetlands, while the water is high.

stories.headline: Ancient DNA Reveals a New Subspecies of New Zealand's Lost Bush Wren
stories.summary: University of Otago researchers used ancient DNA from museum specimens to identify a previously unknown bush wren subspecies, the Tōtaranui bush wren. The work also reshapes the family tree of the wrens, the last of which went extinct in the 1970s.
stories.narrative:
A tiny forest bird that vanished from New Zealand half a century ago has just revealed new secrets, thanks to DNA locked in museum specimens.

The bush wrens were small, ground-dwelling birds. The North Island and South Island forms were gone by 1955 and 1968. The last, Stead's bush wren, disappeared from a small island off Rakiura Stewart Island around 1972, after ship rats reached its final stronghold.

Associate Professor Nic Rawlence and researcher Alexander Verry at the University of Otago studied specimens held in museums around the world. They found that the bush wren family began about six million years ago, as the rising Southern Alps created new habitats, and that Ice Age cycles split the birds into separate lineages. The North and South Island birds diverged about two and a half million years ago, so they should be treated as distinct species.

Genetic sexing also showed that males and females differed in plumage, which scientists had thought they did not. And the team identified a previously unrecognised subspecies in the central and northern South Island, named the Tōtaranui bush wren after the Māori name for Queen Charlotte Sound.

The authors say the lessons from these birds, including the rat invasion that ended them, continue to shape how island predators are managed, and they argue for protecting genetic diversity in species still at risk.

stories.headline: Takahē Chick Hatches at Farewell Spit Just Months After Birds Were Released There
stories.summary: Eight takahē moved from the Heaphy Track to Pūponga on Onetahua/Farewell Spit in May have already formed a new pair and hatched the site's first chick. Conservationists say it is an early sign that the predator-controlled habitat is working.
stories.narrative:
In the north of Golden Bay, at the base of Farewell Spit, a very small bird is giving a big boost to a conservation project. The Department of Conservation has announced that the first takahē chick has hatched at Pūponga, in early October.

The story begins in late May, when eight takahē were moved from Gouland Downs, on the Heaphy Track, to the restoration area. Takahē are the large flightless birds that were once thought to be extinct before a small population was found in Fiordland in 1948. Moving birds to new sites is a key way to grow their numbers.

What has pleased the project team is how quickly things happened. The birds arrived as strangers, formed a new pair, and produced a chick about five months after the move. Staff say that is an excellent start, and one of them simply called it pretty special.

The project is a partnership between Manawhenua ki Mohua, HealthPost Nature Trust, Pest Free Onetahua and DOC. It covers around twelve thousand hectares, with a new predator-resistant fence protecting about two thousand of them. Stoat control is under way and cat control is planned. The area also supports dotterel, kiwi, little blue penguins and migratory shorebirds.

For mana whenua, the return of the bird matters beyond numbers. The chair of Manawhenua ki Mohua said its presence restores the wairua and mauri of the taonga species to Onetahua. Visitors are being asked to watch the takahē from a distance this summer so the chick can grow up undisturbed.

stories.headline: Leukemia Vaccine Extends Survival in Phase 3 Trial, Cutting Risk of Death by 41%
stories.summary: A peptide vaccine for acute myeloid leukemia met its main goal in a pivotal phase 3 trial, with patients living a median 24 months versus 14.7 on standard treatment. It is still investigational, but could become the first off-the-shelf cancer vaccine.
stories.narrative:
A vaccine designed to keep a hard-to-treat blood cancer from coming back has passed a major test. Results announced this week show that the vaccine, called galinpepimut-S, helped people with acute myeloid leukemia live longer in a large phase 3 trial.

The trial, known as REGAL, enrolled 126 patients whose leukemia had returned and who were in a second or later remission but could not have a transplant. Half received the vaccine and half got the best available treatment chosen by their doctors.

The vaccine group lived a median of 24 months, compared with 14.7 months for the others, which works out to a 41 percent lower risk of death. Side effects were mostly mild to moderate, and no new safety concerns appeared.

The vaccine was discovered at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. It trains the immune system to attack cells carrying a protein called WT1, which turns up in more than 95 percent of AML cases. Because it is not made for each patient individually, it could be given widely, and its inventor said the data bring us closer to the first off-the-shelf vaccine for cancer patients.

There are caveats. These are topline results that have not yet been peer reviewed, the vaccine is not approved, and the company plans to discuss filing with the FDA, possibly in 2027. Even so, a randomised phase 3 win for a cancer vaccine is a real milestone for people with few options.

stories.headline: Ladakh's Black-Necked Crane Count Climbs 25% to 108 as Ex-Servicemen Guard Nests
stories.summary: This year's survey in Ladakh counted 108 black-necked cranes, up from 87 in 2025, including 22 juveniles. Officials credit a force of ex-servicemen who protect nests and chicks from free-ranging dogs, alongside local youth.
stories.narrative:
High on the Changthang plateau in Ladakh, the state bird is doing better. The 2026 count of black-necked cranes found 108 birds, up nearly a quarter from 87 last year.

The survey found 86 adults and 22 juveniles, compared with 70 adults and 17 young birds the year before. Chushul had the most cranes with 16, followed by Tsokar and Kargyam with 15 each, and Korzok with 14. Those four sites hold more than half the total.

Officials say the growth is no fluke. Adult numbers rose by roughly 13 percent a year on average from 2021 to 2025. The Lieutenant Governor praised the Environment Protection Force, whose ex-servicemen guard nests, eggs and hatchlings, especially from free-ranging dogs, which are a major threat to ground-nesting birds.

Local communities, particularly young people, have also joined the effort. The official called the increase a monumental milestone for the region. The numbers are still small, so the species stays vulnerable, but a steady rise driven by local protection is a hopeful result.

stories.headline: Bay of Plenty Volunteer Helps Get Free Tracking Devices to People at Risk of Going Missing
stories.summary: Corey Hinde, a Bay of Plenty volunteer with Land Search and Rescue's WanderWell scheme, gives a few hours a month to deliver free radio trackers to people with dementia, autism or disability. About 500 people are on the national database, and searchers can find a wearer even where phone tracking fails.
stories.narrative:
In the Bay of Plenty, a volunteer named Corey Hinde has been named Volunteer of the Month for November for a job that takes only a few hours of his time each month, but can matter enormously to a family.

He works with WanderWell, a New Zealand Land Search and Rescue initiative set up in 2025 to give a consistent, nationwide home to a service that has existed for years. WanderWell provides free small radio transmitters, worn as a pendant, watch or keyring, to people who are at risk of going missing because of dementia, autism or another disability.

If a wearer does go missing, Police and trained search and rescue crews can use specialist equipment to pick up the signal. Because it relies on radio rather than mobile networks, it can work in places where phone-based tracking would not.

Corey's part is the practical side. He receives and activates devices, rings families, arranges delivery, and swaps units out when batteries reach the end of their six-month life. He usually handles three to five devices a month, often bundling visits into a single day. The national database holds about 500 people, with around 30 clients in and around Tauranga.

He says it is not a difficult thing to do, but it is rewarding. The scheme's coordinator says you can literally hear the sigh of relief down the phone when families get a device. The programme is looking for more volunteers in Katikati, Te Puke, Whakatāne and the eastern Bay, and no search and rescue experience or fitness is needed, just reliability, police vetting and a driver's licence.

stories.headline: Algeria Repays Kansas Town's World Cup Welcome With a Trip of a Lifetime
stories.summary: After Lawrence, Kansas warmly hosted Algeria's World Cup team in June, Algeria's president invited a delegation from the town to visit. The group, including the mayor and local police, toured Roman ruins and watched Algeria play.
stories.narrative:
When Algeria's national team chose Lawrence, Kansas as its base for the 2026 World Cup, the town of about 95,000 people rolled out the welcome. Hundreds of Algerian diaspora fans travelled in, organised by a University of Kansas student and her friends through social media pages.

A video of a Lawrence resident thanking Algeria for choosing the city, saying neighbours didn't know much about the country but wanted to make visitors feel at home, was viewed tens of millions of times in June. One local later said the Algerians had adopted them.

In early November, Algeria returned the favour. At the invitation of the country's president, a delegation from Kansas landed in Algiers at 4:30 in the morning to find government and hospitality officials waiting with flowers. The group included Lawrence's mayor, members of the fan group, local police officers who had handled security at the team's training sessions, and residents of Kansas City.

They were given delegation passes and toured sites such as the Roman and Carthaginian ruins at Tipaza, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Royal Mausoleum of Mauretania. They also watched Algeria beat Togo one-nil in an African Cup of Nations qualifier.

It is a simple story: a small town's hospitality to strangers was remembered and repaid in kind.

stories.headline: West Coast's First Recorded Sea Turtle Nests Produce Hatchlings Released Into the Pacific
stories.summary: Olive ridley turtles nested on Southern California beaches for what officials describe as the first recorded time on the U.S. West Coast. With a storm approaching, eggs were moved to the Aquarium of the Pacific, and the hatchlings were released to the ocean over the weekend.
stories.narrative:
In late September, a female olive ridley sea turtle came ashore on a Southern California beach, dug a nest, laid her eggs and slipped back into the sea while lifeguards looked on. A second nest turned up the following day at Huntington Beach, and a third was documented in Ventura County in November. Officials describe these as the first recorded sea turtle nests on the U.S. West Coast.

When storms were forecast, state and federal authorities decided the eggs were at risk and moved them to the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach, where they could be incubated safely. Once the hatchlings emerged, they were carried to beaches in Orange County for release.

Handlers measured each hatchling before letting go, and photographers worked under red or infrared light so the animals would not be disturbed. Then the little turtles did the rest themselves, scrambling across the sand and into the Pacific.

Nobody knows quite why the turtles chose California. An aquarium volunteer director said weather or unusual behaviour hasn't been ruled out, and a Fish and Wildlife Service biologist suggested this year's strong El Niño pattern might be a factor. He also noted that olive ridley populations have increased substantially across parts of their range, crediting decades of conservation work.

That is the good news here: a species once hit hard by fishing and egg collection is recovering enough to try new beaches, and people were on hand to give its youngest arrivals a safe start.

stories.headline: Forever Chemicals Fall About 30% in England's Rivers and 49% in Fish
stories.summary: Environment Agency monitoring shows PFOA and PFOS, two of the most worrying PFAS 'forever chemicals', have dropped roughly 30% in English rivers and by about half in fish. The decline follows bans on the compounds.
stories.narrative:
Two of the best-known forever chemicals, PFOA and PFOS, are turning up in much smaller amounts across England's waterways. Environment Agency monitoring shows river concentrations down roughly 29 to 30 percent, and levels in fish tissue down by around 49 percent.

The two compounds were banned under the Stockholm Convention. Britain all but banned PFOS in 2010 and PFOA in 2020, and other countries have since followed, with France bringing in bans on certain products in January. The new figures suggest those restrictions are working in the real environment.

PFAS are used in waterproof clothing, food packaging, firefighting foam and non-stick pans, and they linger for a very long time. The International Agency for Research on Cancer rates PFOA as carcinogenic to humans, which is why falling levels matter.

The Environment Agency now routinely tests for 60 kinds of PFAS in rivers, lakes, groundwater, coastal waters, fish and shellfish. An environmental forensics researcher at Manchester Metropolitan University told the BBC it was brilliant to see how far things had come in ten years.

The fish result stands out, since it hints that moderate cuts at scale can meaningfully lower what people and wildlife are exposed to.

stories.headline: Auckland Hobbyist's Refurbished Bikes Give Kids a Christmas Present and Families a Ride
stories.summary: Rick Law fixes up secondhand bikes in his north Auckland shed and donates them, with helmets, locks and pumps, to the Rodney Women's Centre. Fifteen are ready for this Christmas.
stories.narrative:
In a shed north of Auckland, Rick Law spends about two hours on each secondhand bike, restoring it to safe riding condition. He began two years ago as a hobby, tracking down unwanted bikes through local Facebook pages, and now delivers three or four batches a year under the name Bikes for Kids.

This Christmas, fifteen refurbished bikes are going to the Rodney Women's Centre, each with a helmet, lock and tyre pump. Sponsors have covered some costs, and Law pays part of the rest himself and does all the repairs.

The centre's manager says the bikes go to mothers buying birthday and Christmas presents, retirees who want exercise, and teenagers who need a way to get to work. Law says he does it for the picture of a child finding a bike under the tree, and he credits locals who respond to his posts.

stories.headline: Earthshot Prize Awards £1 Million Each to Five Climate Solutions in Mumbai
stories.summary: Prince William presented five winners, including Bhutan's forest conservation and a campaign for a PFAS ban in France, with £1 million each. The winners were chosen from 15 finalists.
stories.narrative:
At a ceremony in Mumbai, Prince William presented the Earthshot Prize to five winners, each receiving one million pounds to scale their work. They were picked from fifteen finalists.

The winners were Mahindra Last Mile Mobility, which works on electric transport; PFAS-Free France, a campaign to ban toxic forever chemicals; the Niue Ocean Wide Trust, which protects marine ecosystems; the energy company Ørsted for offshore wind; and Bhutan, honoured for conserving its Himalayan forests, the only country among the winners.

The prize, founded by William through his Royal Foundation in 2020, is aimed at practical solutions to environmental problems. The money gives proven projects the means to grow, and the Niue and Bhutan wins recognise conservation led by small nations.

stories.headline: Fibre Supplement Improves Gut Health in People With IBS in Randomised Trial
stories.summary: An Edith Cowan University trial found a resistant starch and psyllium fibre supplement improved gut bacteria in people with irritable bowel syndrome without worsening symptoms. Gut-related anxiety also decreased.
stories.narrative:
Researchers at Edith Cowan University in Australia ran a randomised, double-blind trial of a fibre supplement in people with irritable bowel syndrome who were following a low-FODMAP diet. That diet can help symptoms but often starves the gut of fibre.

The supplement combined resistant starch with psyllium husk. Participants kept stable symptoms, with no worsening of pain, bloating, diarrhoea or constipation, while their gut bacteria improved markedly over a short period. Gut-related anxiety also fell.

One researcher said changes of this size are rarely seen with such a short intervention. The team stresses that more research is needed on wider effects, but the result suggests a safe way to restore fibre for millions of IBS sufferers. It was published in the European Journal of Nutrition.

stories.headline: Gentle Bursts of Pink Noise During Sleep Boost the Brain's Waste-Clearing Fluid Waves, MIT Study Finds
stories.summary: MIT researchers showed that quiet 50-millisecond bursts of pink noise, timed to slow brain waves, made the waves of cerebrospinal fluid that flush the brain larger in 14 healthy volunteers. The sounds were soft enough not to wake sleepers. It opens a route to non-drug ways of supporting sleep, memory and possibly protection against Alzheimer's.
stories.narrative:
Researchers at MIT have found a gentle way to nudge the brain's overnight cleaning system. During deep sleep, the brain produces slow electrical waves, and these are followed by pulses of cerebrospinal fluid that wash through the brain and help carry away waste.

The team, led by Laura Lewis and lead author Joshua Levitt, played very short bursts of pink noise, a sound with extra energy at low pitches, timed to land right at the peaks of those slow waves. A prediction algorithm worked out when the next peak would arrive, and a custom method cleaned up the interference between EEG and MRI recordings in under a tenth of a second.

In fourteen healthy volunteers, the sound bursts made the slow waves stronger, and the fluid waves that follow them grew larger too. The sounds were quiet enough that sleepers were not woken.

The researchers are careful to say that they have not yet shown more waste is actually removed, or that sleep quality improves. Their next steps are testing people with insomnia, and looking at memory and at the clearance of proteins linked to Alzheimer's disease, such as amyloid beta and tau.

The good news is the idea itself: a simple, non-invasive, drug-free way to support the brain's natural housekeeping. Levitt has already started a company exploring a possible home device, perhaps something like a headband. The work was published in Science Translational Medicine.

stories.headline: Hawke's Bay Vet Opens a Working-Farm Classroom So Town Kids Can Meet Calves and Collect Eggs
stories.summary: Vet and farmer Sally Newall has grown her Kiwi Country Kids social media project to more than 26,000 followers. She is now building a barn on her Pātoka farm where schools and families can feed animals, watch milking and make butter. She hopes seeing real farm life will build trust between town and country.
stories.narrative:
Sally Newall is a vet and farmer who runs a 500-hectare farm at Pātoka, north of Napier. In 2020 she began a social media project called Kiwi Country Kids to show people what working farm life is really like. It now has more than 26,000 followers, from current and former farmers to town dwellers with no farming link at all.

Now she is taking the project off the screen. Beside the family homestead she has built a three-bay barn that doubles as a learning space. One side has a milking and wet area, the middle is a covered room for workshops and school visits, and the other side holds calf pens that also serve the working farm. A women's butchery night has already been held there.

Visitors can feed animals, collect eggs, watch a cow being milked and make butter, and meet goats, pigs, sheep, horses, and even rescued commercial hens. The calves are a mix of Charolais and Friesian, only days to a month old, and Newall's years as a vet help them settle in.

She says getting people onto the farm matters more now that AI-generated videos can blur what's real. Her aim is to show people that farmers care about their animals and the environment. It is a small, hands-on way of bridging town and country.

stories.headline: Māori Queen Makes Historic First Poukai Visit to Tairāwhiti
stories.summary: Te Arikinui Kuini Ngā wai hono i te pō visited Gisborne for the region's first Poukai, welcomed by more than 200 people performing a haka pōwhiri. The visit was requested by Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki two years ago. It featured a museum exhibition, mokopapa and a communal feast.
stories.narrative:
The Māori Queen, Te Arikinui Kuini Ngā wai hono i te pō, has made the first Poukai visit to Tairāwhiti. A Poukai is an annual circuit of marae connected to the Kiingitanga, a tradition dating back to the reign of the second Māori King, Tāwhiao.

The iwi Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki asked for a Poukai in their region two years ago, and the Kiingitanga agreed the following year. Over the weekend, more than two hundred people performed a haka pōwhiri to welcome the Queen to Te Poho o Rāwiri Marae in Gisborne.

The celebrations included an exhibition at the Tairāwhiti Museum, participants receiving mokopapa, traditional facial tattoos, and a communal feast with song and haka. Kiingitanga spokesperson Rahui Papa called the occasion absolutely beautiful.

He pointed to the long ties between the Kiingitanga and Te Aitanga-a-Māhaki, including the role of their leader Te Kani te Ua in choosing Te Arikinui Te Atairangikaahu in 1966. He also said young people were heavily involved in setting up the Poukai and will carry its teachings forward.

stories.headline: Pacific and Māori Medical Admission Scheme MAPAS Marks 50 Years, With Graduates Now Working in Hospitals
stories.summary: The MAPAS pathway into medicine at Auckland has helped Māori and Pacific students become doctors for over 50 years. Past and present graduates gathered to honour Professor Colin Mantell. Supporters say graduates are more likely to become GPs and work in rural areas.
stories.narrative:
For more than fifty years, the Māori and Pacific Admission Scheme, known as MAPAS, has helped Māori and Pacific students into healthcare study at the University of Auckland. This week, generations of health leaders gathered at Waipapa Taumata Rau to honour Emeritus Professor Colin Mantell, whose work helped shape the scheme.

The need is clear. Māori make up under six percent of the medical workforce but about eighteen percent of the population, and Pacific representation among doctors is lower still. Life expectancy gaps are around six to seven years.

Joseph Johnston, a Samoan doctor who graduated through MAPAS in 2025, is now a first-year house officer at Waitākere Hospital. He is heading to Middlemore next year and wants to become a surgeon. Current students describe the scheme as levelling the playing field, in the words of one, bringing everyone to the same starting point.

Professor David Tipene-Leach says graduates pass at the same rates as others, tend to stay in New Zealand, and are more likely to become GPs and work in rural areas. The scheme remains politically contested, but the story is of a pipeline that has been turning out doctors for half a century.

stories.headline: Doctors Use Marrow From a Deceased Organ Donor to Treat Severe Aplastic Anemia in a First
stories.summary: A 40-year-old woman with a decade-long blood disorder received a transplant of bone marrow recovered from a deceased organ donor. Six months on, the marrow has taken hold, her blood counts have recovered and she no longer needs transfusions.
stories.narrative:
Doctors at Franciscan Health in the American Midwest have reported what they believe is the first transplant of bone marrow from a deceased organ donor used to treat severe aplastic anemia, a condition in which the body stops making enough blood cells.

The patient is a 40-year-old woman who had lived with the disease for ten years. Her condition had been stable for a time, but it worsened despite several treatments and stopped responding to medication, leaving her in need of a transplant.

On April 18, her team transplanted marrow that had been recovered from a deceased organ donor and stored by a marrow bank run by Ossium Health. Six months later, the results are striking. The donor cells have taken hold and now produce all of her blood and immune cells, a state called full donor chimerism. Her blood counts have recovered, and she no longer needs blood or platelet transfusions. There were no complications reported.

Marrow transplants for this disease have been done since the 1970s, but they have relied on living donors, which means patients must find a match among relatives or volunteers. Drawing on marrow from organ donors could widen the pool of available matches. The treating physician, Dr Felix Mensah, said this appears to be the first reported case of its kind for severe aplastic anemia.

Ossium says it plans to support more such transplants, for both cancers and non-cancerous conditions. It is a single case, but it points to a new route to a cure for people who struggle to find a donor.

stories.headline: Two of the Pacific's Last Untouched Atolls Become the Marshall Islands' First National Marine Sanctuary
stories.summary: Bikar and Bokak, remote atolls surveyed as some of the most intact ecosystems on Earth, now anchor a sanctuary covering about 18,500 square miles. Surveys found abundant sharks, seabird colonies and species new to the country.
stories.narrative:
Two remote coral atolls in the northern Marshall Islands, Bikar and Bokak, have been protected as part of the country's first national marine sanctuary, covering some 18,500 square miles of ocean.

Scientists describe the atolls as among the last wild and healthy ecosystems in the region, and possibly the world. They lie far from anywhere people live, and the community of Utirik Atoll has looked after them for decades.

A research effort that began in 2023 surveyed land, reef, deep sea and sky. Teams used scuba, underwater video, deep-sea cameras and even a submarine. They counted more than a dozen breeding seabird colonies, hundreds of groups of reef fish, dozens of deep-sea fish groups and open-water predators such as sharks, jacks and wahoo.

Fourteen of the groups they recorded had not been seen in the Marshall Islands before, and two may be new to science. The findings were published in Frontiers in Marine Science, led by marine ecologist Alan Friedlander of the University of Hawaii.

The sanctuary was declared two years after the assessment, turning that knowledge into lasting protection. It is good news because it locks in safe habitat for a rare, healthy reference ecosystem, protected before it was damaged rather than after.

stories.headline: King Charles's Farms to Trial Southland Deer Farmer's Edible Bale Netting
stories.summary: Orepuki deer farmer Grant Lightfoot invented a jute baleage netting that livestock can safely eat, replacing plastic netting. After meeting Prince William in the UK, he has left a roll for the King's farms to test.
stories.narrative:
A Southland deer farmer's idea for a plastic-free farm product has caught the attention of the British royal family.

Grant Lightfoot, from Orepuki, invented Kiwi Econet, a baleage netting made from jute. Plastic netting inside baleage and silage bales can end up eaten by livestock, so his version is made from a material animals can digest safely. It doesn't replace the outer plastic wrap, but it removes one source of plastic from the farm.

The idea came to him while he was working as a commercial diver and sitting in a decompression chamber, thinking about his home farm. The first prototype was 50 metres long, hand-knitted from jute twine with his partner Colleen Quirk at roughly a metre a night, which took weeks.

After meeting Lightfoot at the Groundswell Festival in the UK, Prince William showed interest, telling him it would be really good on their farms. Lightfoot followed up with the King's farm manager and left a roll, and the royal farms are due to trial it over the coming season.

It is a small invention from a small southern town, now headed for testing on one of the most watched farms in Britain.

stories.headline: Wellington Town Hall Nears Reopening After 13 Years, With a New National Music Centre
stories.summary: The earthquake-strengthened Town Hall, with its restored 1906 organ, reopens on 20 February 2027. It will host the NZ Symphony Orchestra and give university music students a home alongside professionals.
stories.narrative:
After 13 years boarded up, Wellington Town Hall is in the final phase of its upgrade and has a reopening date: 20 February 2027, with a sold-out show from Drax Project and Bret McKenzie.

The building was declared earthquake prone in 2013. It stands on reclaimed land with old unreinforced concrete piles, and a stream runs beneath it. Engineers lifted and base-isolated it, a job the programme manager called one of the most complex strengthening projects in New Zealand history, all while protecting the hall's acoustics and heritage.

The budget grew from around 43 million dollars to nearly 330 million, but the final phase now looks likely to come in about 20 million under the latest figure.

Inside, the 121-year-old Adam Auditorium and its 1906 organ have been restored, and a new entrance carries light installations inspired by mana whenua and coastal design.

The hall will become a National Music Centre, a partnership between Victoria University of Wellington's school of music and the New Zealand Symphony Orchestra, which will be based there 135 days a year. Students will rehearse and perform alongside professionals, and one young trombonist said the space could inspire his generation of musicians.

stories.headline: Tiny One-Gram Trackers Let Scientists Follow Nationally Critical Long-Tailed Bats Through Fiordland Nights
stories.summary: The Department of Conservation is fitting long-tailed bats with raisin-weight tags that report each bat's position every 30 seconds. Bat numbers in the Eglinton valley are already rising thanks to predator control, and the new data should help target protection even better.
stories.narrative:
In Fiordland's Eglinton valley, conservation staff now have a new way to watch one of New Zealand's rarest mammals. The Department of Conservation is attaching tiny tracking tags to long-tailed bats, which carry the country's highest threat ranking, Nationally Critical.

Tracking bats has always been hard. Older tags could only be followed on foot or by vehicle, and the bats, which can cover up to forty kilometres in a night, simply outran the people chasing them. Worse, the animals weigh at most about twelve grams, so any device had to be extraordinarily light.

The new tags weigh about one gram, roughly a raisin, and are about the size of a little fingernail. Each one sends a simple pulse that is picked up by twenty fixed base stations around the valley, and a central server works out where the bat is. Researchers get a location every thirty seconds for around twelve days, depending on battery life.

The system was piloted on seven bats last summer. This summer the team, working under a three-year programme called Bats Beyond Borders with support from Air New Zealand, plans to track sixty. Local landowners are hosting some of the base stations.

The encouraging backdrop is that long-tailed and short-tailed bat numbers in the Eglinton valley are rising, which has been linked to years of rat and stoat control. Researchers hope the new movement data will show where the bats feed and roost, so predator control and habitat protection can be aimed exactly where they matter most.

stories.headline: China's Emissions Fall 3.1% in Third Quarter, Biggest Quarterly Drop Since 2022, as Clean Power and EVs Surge
stories.summary: Analysis for Carbon Brief finds China's CO2 emissions fell 3.1% in the third quarter, extending a flat-or-falling trend since March 2024. Solar, wind and nuclear added more than twice the growth in electricity demand, and electric vehicles hit 67% of car sales in September.
stories.narrative:
China, the world's largest emitter, has just recorded its biggest quarterly fall in carbon dioxide emissions since the Covid lockdowns of 2022. An analysis by Lauri Myllyvirta of the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, published by Carbon Brief, puts the third-quarter drop at 3.1 percent.

The fall is part of a longer pattern. Emissions have been flat or falling since March 2024, and so far this year they are estimated to be down half a percent. Coal use fell about three percent compared with a year earlier, and oil use fell about four percent.

Clean energy did much of the work. Solar, wind and nuclear generation grew by 110 terawatt-hours, more than twice the growth in total electricity demand, so coal plants simply ran less. Less clean power was also being wasted through grid curtailment.

Transport was the other big factor. Oil used in transport dropped nine percent, as electric vehicles reached a record 67 percent of passenger car sales in September and half of heavy truck sales. Electricity used by EVs grew 53 percent.

The author cautions that mild weather and weaker construction, which cut cement and steel emissions, also played a part, and that what happens next depends on policy and economic growth. Even so, a clear shift from growth to decline in the biggest emitter is a genuinely encouraging sign for the climate.

stories.headline: China Switches On the World's Largest Liquid-Air Energy Storage Plant
stories.summary: A 60-megawatt, 600-megawatt-hour plant in Qinghai Province now stores surplus renewable power by chilling air into a liquid. It can supply about ten hours of electricity when the sun and wind fade, using no lithium.
stories.narrative:
China has switched on what is described as the largest liquid-air energy storage plant in the world, in Qinghai Province in the west of the country. It can deliver 60 megawatts of power and hold 600 megawatt-hours of energy, enough to run for roughly ten hours.

The idea is simple to describe. When electricity is plentiful, machines draw in air, compress it and chill it to around minus 190 degrees Celsius, until it becomes a liquid that is kept in insulated tanks. When the grid needs power, the liquid is pumped to high pressure and warmed. It expands back into gas, spins a turbine and feeds electricity into the grid. Heat and cold produced along the way are stored and reused, which cuts waste.

The plant was developed by a state-owned investment group working with the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and it sits alongside a 250 megawatt solar farm in a region with strong sun and wind. Storage is the missing piece that lets renewables keep supplying power after dark or on still days, so a large working demonstration matters.

The report notes that a first commercial-scale liquid-air project is planned in Vermont, and the Qinghai plant has about twenty percent more capacity than that one. Analysts quoted say the technology can be much cheaper per unit stored than lithium-ion batteries, and it relies on air rather than scarce minerals. A working plant at this scale is a real step toward cheap, long-duration storage.

stories.headline: Actor, 85, Takes to the Stage in Beckett Despite Alzheimer's Diagnosis
stories.summary: Peter Marinker, diagnosed with Alzheimer's, performed Krapp's Last Tape in London with practical support from his team. The run raised money for the Alzheimer's Society.
stories.narrative:
Peter Marinker, an actor of 85, has returned to the London stage in Samuel Beckett's Krapp's Last Tape, a demanding solo play, after being diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease.

He found out about the condition after struggling during rehearsals for an earlier production. Rather than retire, he kept working. The production gave him practical help: an autocue, an earpiece for prompts, and extra rehearsal time. It also drew on recordings of his own 1983 performance of the same role.

The play is about an old man listening to tapes of his younger self, and Marinker says that fits his situation, as people increasingly lean on gadgets to remember things. He describes his thinking as shifting towards intuition and feeling, and says he is reaching back into his past to help himself in the present.

The director, Dave Wybrow, says the show exists because of Peter's Alzheimer's, not in spite of it, since memory and identity are at the heart of the play. The four-day run at the Cockpit Theatre raised money for the Alzheimer's Society, and shows that a diagnosis need not end a creative life.

stories.headline: Lost Georgia O'Keeffe Painting Found in a Manhattan Closet Heads to Auction
stories.summary: A woman clearing her late aunt's East Village apartment found a 1930 O'Keeffe landscape in its original box. Christie's expects about $3 million; the aunt paid $3,800 in 1963.
stories.narrative:
A long-lost Georgia O'Keeffe painting has turned up in a closet in a Manhattan apartment. The oil, Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I, dates from 1930 and shows rolling hills.

A woman identified only as Betsy found it after the death of her aunt, a former foreign service member. The aunt had bought it in 1963 for 3,800 dollars, and had once remarked that there was an O'Keeffe in the closet. She apparently moved it out of sight after noticing a bridge-game guest staring at it.

The painting was still in its original gallery box. Experts authenticated it through the box, the artist's signature on the back, and a 1931 photograph by her husband, Alfred Stieglitz.

Christie's believes it is probably the first of about three paintings O'Keeffe made of the New Mexico hills after her first trip there in 1929. It goes to auction on November 17 with an estimate of around 3 million dollars. The specialist handling it called the discovery a once-in-a-lifetime moment.

stories.headline: Fiordland National Park Becomes the Southern Hemisphere's Largest International Dark Sky Park
stories.summary: Fiordland National Park has been accredited by DarkSky International, covering 12,607 square kilometres and making it the largest dark sky park in the Southern Hemisphere. It is Southland's second dark sky place after Stewart Island Rakiura.
stories.narrative:
Fiordland National Park has just been officially recognised as an International Dark Sky Park, and it is a big one. At 12,607 square kilometres, it is the largest in the Southern Hemisphere and the third largest in the world.

The accreditation comes from DarkSky International and follows years of work between the regional development agency Great South, the Department of Conservation and others. That work included measuring sky quality and improving public lighting so the natural darkness over the park is protected.

It is the second dark sky place in Southland, after Stewart Island Rakiura was accredited in 2019. DarkSky International's president, New Zealander Nalayini Brito-Davies, wrote the nomination letter after walking the Milford Track, and she is pushing for the country to become a Dark Sky Nation.

The benefits go beyond stargazing. DOC says dark skies help native species, and the night sky also carries cultural weight, including its place in Matariki. Work continues on monitoring, light management and education, and there are efforts to write dark sky protection into future district planning.

stories.headline: Chile's Atacama Desert Erupts in Its Biggest Wildflower Bloom in Decades
stories.summary: Heavy El Niño rains have woken millions of dormant seeds and bulbs in the world's driest non-polar desert, producing over 200 flowering species. The bloom is the largest in 30 years and possibly ever, and Chile's seed bank is collecting specimens.
stories.narrative:
The Atacama Desert in northern Chile, the driest non-polar desert on Earth, is covered in pink, yellow, lilac and purple flowers. Locals call it the Desierto Florido, and this year's display is the largest and most colourful in around 30 years, and possibly ever.

The cause was heavy winter rain linked to El Niño. Some areas had their wettest conditions since records began in the 1950s, and the water soaked deeper than it has in decades. That woke millions of seeds, bulbs and tubers that had lain dormant, and more than 200 species are flowering, some in patches where flowers have never been recorded.

The bloom brings a short-lived ecosystem with it. Insects hatch, lizards and bats follow, and larger animals such as guanacos benefit. The crimson garra de leon, found along only a few miles of this coast and nowhere else, is among the stars.

Scientists are also acting. Chile's national seed bank is collecting specimens to preserve genetic material, and the park administrator describes the desert as a natural seed bank. The regional governor is seeking UNESCO World Heritage recognition, and tourism is expected to bring around 300,000 overnight trips. The bloom should last until about mid-November.

stories.headline: Archaeologists Find 280 Ice Age Engravings Hidden in Plain Sight in a Catalan Cave
stories.summary: Researchers have identified about 280 engravings, roughly 26,000 years old, in Spain's Font Major cave, which tourists have walked through since 1957. The find is the third-largest Ice Age engraving collection on the Mediterranean side of Iberia and shows Catalonia was not the empty region it appeared.
stories.narrative:
Archaeologists in Catalonia, Spain, have found around 280 Ice Age engravings in the Font Major cave system, in a section that has been open to visitors since 1957. Generations of people walked past them without noticing.

The team from the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution spotted them during excavations in 2019, and the results were published in the journal Antiquity. The images include 55 distinct animals, among them horses, a bear, deer and early wild cattle, plus dozens of abstract lines and loops.

Radiocarbon dating of charcoal found in an engraved groove puts the art at about 26,000 years old. The researchers think lighting is why it was missed: the carvings are hard to see when light hits them head on.

The discovery matters because Catalonia had very little known Ice Age art compared with neighbouring regions in France and northern Spain. This collection is the third largest on the Mediterranean side of the Iberian Peninsula, and its style differs from that of nearby regions, so it opens up new questions about how people lived and expressed themselves there.

stories.headline: Brown Bear Population in Spain Doubles as Its Breeding Range Expands
stories.summary: Cantabrian brown bears in northern Spain have roughly doubled from about 140 to about 370 over two decades, and now occupy over 17,000 square kilometres. Protected areas, tougher penalties for killing bears and rural depopulation helped.
stories.narrative:
Europe's largest land carnivore is doing well in northern Spain. The Cantabrian brown bear population has roughly doubled over about twenty years, from around 140 animals to about 370.

Their range has grown too, and they now occupy more than 17,000 square kilometres across Asturias, Leon, Galicia, Palencia and Cantabria. Two breeding groups that were once separate now overlap, which is important for the genetic health of the population.

The recovery followed a low point in the 1980s and 1990s, when numbers fell by a quarter. Researchers credit government protection, new protected areas such as Somiedo Natural Park and Redes National Park, heavy fines for illegally killing bears, and people leaving rural areas, which freed up habitat.

There is room to grow, since Asturias alone has about 5,000 square kilometres of suitable habitat the bears could move into. The study's authors say management plans should now be updated to support that.

stories.headline: Newborn Deaths Fell by Half in Flint After Cash Program for New Parents Launched
stories.summary: A study in JAMA Pediatrics found neonatal mortality in Flint, Michigan dropped 50% in the first year of Rx Kids, a program giving families cash during pregnancy and infancy. Deaths in the first week of life fell 74%, while the rest of Michigan stayed flat.
stories.narrative:
In Flint, Michigan, a city long burdened by poverty and a water crisis, researchers say the number of babies dying in their first month of life has fallen by half.

The finding comes from a study in JAMA Pediatrics led by Michigan State University's Mona Hanna, who also directs the program in question. Called Rx Kids, it was the first community-wide cash prescription scheme for mothers and babies in the United States. Every family gets fifteen hundred dollars during pregnancy and five hundred dollars a month through the baby's first year.

Comparing statewide birth and death records from 2021 to 2025, the team found that neonatal mortality in Flint dropped from about ten per thousand live births to about five in the first year after launch. Deaths in the first seven days fell even more sharply, by 74 percent. Over the same period the rest of Michigan barely changed. Before the program Flint's rate was more than double the state's; now the gap is no longer statistically significant.

An earlier study had already found fewer preterm births, fewer low birth weight babies and fewer admissions to neonatal intensive care in Flint, which are leading causes of newborn death. The researchers suggest the money may help through steadier housing, less food hardship, better maternal mental health, more prenatal visits, and families buying safe sleeping gear like cribs.

The study is observational, so it can't prove the cash caused the drop, and the team plans to follow more years and other Rx Kids communities. Still, it's a striking early sign that a simple, low-cost support can help more babies live in a city that has seen more than its share of hardship.

stories.headline: Ten-Year Ban on Scallop Dredging Brings Scotland's Summer Isles Seabed and Fish Back to Life
stories.summary: A decade after industrial scallop dredging was banned around the Summer Isles off north-west Scotland, ancient beds of pink maerl seaweed have survived and fish, dolphins and whales are thriving. The protection was won by a coalition of citizen scientists, activists and small-boat creel fishermen.
stories.narrative:
Off the north-west coast of Scotland, a stretch of sea around the Summer Isles is showing what happens when a seabed is simply left alone. Ten years ago, industrial scallop dredging was banned across roughly 150,000 acres there, and the result is now being described by locals as a change from night to day.

The star of the story is maerl, a hard pink seaweed that grows on the seabed in thick, coral-like beds. Two of the beds in the area stretch for more than a mile, and they have been growing in the same place for around nine thousand years. Maerl matters because it is a nursery: herring, cod and haddock breed among it, and scallops and many other creatures shelter in its tangled structure.

It is also astonishingly fragile. A single pass of heavy dredging gear can crush or bury about seventy percent of the maerl it touches, and it grows back only over centuries. Campaigners say that without the ban, much of it would probably be gone by now.

The protection came about through the Blue Hope Alliance, a coalition of citizen scientists, local activists and an association of creel fishermen, who fish with small baited pots and cause far less damage. Local artist and activist Diyanna Ross called the outcome the most amazing thing to happen to the Summer Isles. Scallop diver Alasdair Hughson, who works with the creel fishermen's federation, said the recovery he has seen underwater is night to day.

Today, whales, dolphins and porpoises are reported to be thriving in the area, and key fish stocks are healthy. Scotland holds roughly thirty percent of the maerl beds in north-west Europe, so keeping this patch intact is good news well beyond one stretch of coast. It is a rare example of a community winning protection for the sea, and then living long enough to see it work.

stories.headline: Teen Teaches Himself Machine Learning and Builds a Free App Helping Families Read Autistic Children's Cues
stories.summary: New Jersey student Shashank Madala built Kora, a free app that suggests possible readings of an autistic child's emotions and how to respond. It is now used by more than 700 people in 12 countries and won a Congressional App Challenge.
stories.narrative:
Shashank Madala was fifteen, with just one computer science class behind him, when he decided to build something for his younger cousin. His cousin is autistic, and at family gatherings the adults around him often misread his upset moments. Shashank taught himself machine learning and created an app called Kora.

Kora is free. A parent or caregiver uses it to see possible readings of how a child may be feeling, such as happy, sad, angry, afraid or neutral, along with suggestions for how to respond. It deliberately gives no scores, diagnoses or judgments.

The design changed after an early lesson. The first version gave one confident answer, and Shashank realised it was repeating the very mistake that had frustrated his cousin: certainty where there should be curiosity. He rebuilt it to offer several possible readings and to flag when it is unsure.

The app now has more than 700 users in twelve countries, mostly reached through autism therapy centres. In December 2025 it took first place in the Congressional App Challenge for New Jersey's tenth district, out of about 4,600 participants, and it was displayed in the US Capitol. In 2026 the New Jersey Senate and General Assembly honoured him with a joint resolution.

He now leads a small team of three colleagues and hopes to bring Kora to more therapy centres, schools and families. It is a lovely example of a young person turning a family worry into practical help for hundreds of others.

stories.headline: Kaiteriteri Becomes Kaiteretere as Name Change Follows Return of Land to Nelson Tenths Owners
stories.summary: The New Zealand Geographic Board has replaced the spelling Kaiteriteri with Kaiteretere, as part of the Nelson Tenths settlement. Customary landowners welcomed the change, which recognises their language and follows the return of 3,068 hectares to them.
stories.narrative:
A well-known Tasman holiday spot is getting its name back. The New Zealand Geographic Board has revoked the long-used spelling Kaiteriteri and replaced it with Kaiteretere, a change made through the legislation settling the Nelson Tenths case.

That legislation, the Te Here ā Nuku bill, passed in August. It returns 3,068 hectares to the original customary owners, including the Kaiteriteri Recreation Reserve and part of the Abel Tasman Great Walk, along with 420 million dollars in compensation. Public access to the reserve and the walk is being kept.

The background is a long-running grievance. In the 1830s the Crown promised Māori would keep one-tenth of the land sold to the New Zealand Company around Nelson. What was actually set aside fell far short, fewer than 3,000 acres of reserves, and the families involved have been seeking redress for generations.

Trustee Kerensa Johnston of the Te Here ā Nuku Trust said the corrected spelling recognises the customary owners' language and tikanga. She noted that official records have used the other spelling since 1859, while surveyors recorded several variants, and that the name is usually understood as kai, to eat, and teretere, to run or spread about. Responses have been mostly positive, though some businesses have raised the cost of changing signs, and the trust plans to make the changes over the next year.

It is a satisfying step in a settlement that is giving land and, now, the proper name of a place back to the people it belongs to.

stories.headline: Unknown Right Whale Calf Found Off Canada Makes 24 Births This Season, the Best Since 2009
stories.summary: Researchers photographed a previously unrecorded North Atlantic right whale calf with its mother off Quebec's Anticosti Island. It lifts the season's tally to 24 calves, the most productive year since 2009 for a species numbering only about 380.
stories.narrative:
Scientists have found a baby whale that nobody knew existed, and it makes this a bumper year for one of the rarest large animals on Earth. In September, researchers in Canada photographed an unrecorded North Atlantic right whale calf swimming beside its mother off Anticosti Island in Quebec.

The mother is a 38-year-old whale known to researchers as Silt. She had been seen in the calving grounds off the south-eastern United States in February, so the calf was probably born there and had left before the pair were documented together. Boat and aerial surveys along the US East Coast all spring and summer had missed it.

The surprise find brings the number of calves from the latest birthing season to 24. According to the New England Aquarium, that is the most productive year for the species since 2009 and the fourth-highest count on record.

That matters because right whales are in a precarious position. Only about 380 remain in the world, and their numbers have been falling since 2010. Each new calf is a real addition to a population that cannot afford losses.

Scientists described the discovery as a cause for joy. Challenges remain, including criticism of moves to delay new protections, but for now there is one more young whale in the Atlantic than anyone thought.

stories.headline: Puhoi Volunteer Fire Brigade Named National Volunteer Brigade of the Year, a First for the Town
